newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway cuts key interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Norway cuts key interest rates.

text.p: Norway's central bank said Tuesday it was cutting key interest rates for the second time in eight months in a bid to rein in the strong crown.

The bank said it was trimming its overnight deposit rate, which sets the floor for money market rates, to 4 percent from 4.5 percent. The overnight lending rate, charged to commercial and savings banks, was cut to 6 percent from 6.5 percent.

The crown has strengthened rapidly because of soaring oil prices and relatively higher rates in Norway than other European countries. Norway is the world's second-biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia.
Central Bank Governor Kjell Storvik said in a statement the decision came in response to recent developments in the money and foreign exchange markets.
"The crown exchange rate has been under persistent pressure and the Norwegian Bank has purchased considerable amounts of foreign currency to curb the rise in the crown," Storvik said.
"A reduction in Norges Bank's interest rates now seemed appropriate to reduce the appreciation pressure."
The bank has sold more than 60 billion Norwegian crowns ($9.5 billion) on the foreign exchange markets so far this year, to curb the crown's rise and to cover investments into the state oil fund.

"I am not very surprised, but I had thought they would hold out a bit longer," said Marius Loemo, economist at Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse. "But it is clear that the crowns's strength had started approaching levels where it is difficult to say it is compatible with a stable currency."
A stronger crown tends to hurt Norwegian exports.
The central bank last trimmed rates on March 7 by a quarter point, the first cut in key rates since February 1994. The latest cuts will be effective on Wednesday.
